A creative tool with a complete loop: make your own water-sort level, try it by hand, and inspect a shortest checked solution.

Open the studio

The problem

A solver report tells you how one supplied puzzle behaves. A level designer needs to change the puzzle, make mistakes, test a move, and try again. PourLab brings those steps into one browser workbench without an installation or account.

The project grows from an earlier independent Python puzzle-analysis prototype. The JavaScript app is a new implementation with interactive editing, manual play, isolated search, checked playback and portable levels. It was built with AI coding assistance.

Try it with your own level

  1. In Create, choose a color and paint the lowest empty slot. Fill bottles bottom to top. Use the eraser or Undo to revise.
  2. Balance every used color to a multiple of the capacity. The inventory explains what needs fixing. Add empty bottles when you need room.
  3. In Play, select a source, then a target. A legal pour transfers the largest top run that fits into an empty bottle or onto the same color.
  4. Choose Analyze original level to solve the original design, regardless of progress in your manual play session. Review every checked move with the slider or playback.
  5. Save a named copy, export JSON, or share a link containing the level. Browser saves stay on this device and origin.

The goal: full bottles containing one color, plus empty bottles. Small numbers identify the colors throughout, so the puzzle does not rely on color alone.

Why exact search?

Each legal pour has a cost of one. Breadth-first search explores by move count; A* uses a lower bound based on the number of separate color segments. Both methods find a shortest route under the same maximal-pour rules. Search treats bottle permutations as equivalent while retaining the real bottle indices for replay.

This is classical pathfinding, not a trained model or reinforcement learning. A shortest route is a useful design signal; it is not a measured prediction of how hard a puzzle feels to a person.

A stopped search is an open question

The app limits states, elapsed time and path depth. Large valid levels can reach a limit. It reports a solution only after legal replay; it reports impossibility only after exhausting the complete reachable space. Reaching a budget or pressing Stop leaves this run unresolved.

Search runs in a real Web Worker to keep the page interactive. Editing cancels a running search and removes the old solution. The main thread verifies the returned path again before displaying it.

What is checked

The test suite compares A* and canonical BFS with a separately implemented, labeled-bottle BFS oracle. It covers exhaustive small arrangements, 16 seeded novel levels, legal replay, inventory conservation, immutable transitions, trapped puzzles, zero-move goals and search limits. Portable-input tests include a hostile HTML-like name that must survive as literal text.

These checks establish behavior on the tested corpus. They do not establish player demand, commercial value, complete accessibility or unaided coding ability. The next useful study is simple: watch an unfamiliar person create, repair, save and share a puzzle, and see where they stop.

Keep your levels portable

A single level can be imported from JSON. A library backup contains up to 50 named levels. Structurally valid incomplete levels remain editable drafts; Play and search wait until their inventory is balanced.

{
  "name": "Three-color study",
  "capacity": 3,
  "bottles": [[0,1,2],[1,2,0],[2,0,1],[],[]]
}

Arrays run bottom to top. JSON color indices 0–7 appear as 1–8 on the board. Import rejects unknown fields, unsupported versions, malformed types and oversized input. Names are rendered as text, never HTML.

No level is uploaded by this app. A copied URL includes the level in its hash and can be opened by anyone who has it. Export a JSON backup before clearing browser data.

Design and credits

PourLab is a playful puzzle instrument: a deep violet stage, bright numbered liquid, physical rounded controls and a working board at the center. The large condensed type and the quiet UI type have different jobs. Create, Play and Review have distinct active colors, while their controls keep the same positions. The palette and search tools sit in a separate lilac console below the board.

Two actual Cosmos references informed the direction: Michael Redfearn’s playful mobile interface for vivid rounded action shapes on a dark stage, and Whipsaw’s Sound Workshop instrument for tactile controls and clear functional grouping. These were inspected as static references; no demonstrated motion timing or asset license was inferred. No Cosmos artwork or code is included.

Barlow Condensed Bold and Manrope are hosted locally under their respective Barlow SIL Open Font License and Manrope SIL Open Font License. Bottles, interface geometry and the drop mark are original CSS/SVG. The active app has no third-party JavaScript runtime dependency. The earlier glass hero and its vendored Three.js are retained only as historical source; neither is loaded by the studio or this guide.

Motion explains a real selection, mode change or legal pour. It does not delay the game state or simulate fluid physics. The visible Motion control can turn feedback off, and reduced-motion visitors start with it off. GOV.UK’s validation guidance informed actionable errors. These design references and engineering checks do not establish player demand or complete accessibility.

Checking the current instrument

The redesigned studio was checked on desktop and at 390px width. A custom capacity-two, three-color level ran through the actual worker: 4 shortest checked pours and 17 A* states in the observed run. Illegal moves, Undo, replay to 4/4, invalid inventory, motion preferences and named save/reload were exercised. These are synthetic functional observations. Current findings and screenshots.
